clinical_application_and_analysis_part.caa7_association_analysis: Predictive modeling using logistic regression (LR), random forest (RF), and XGBoost with 5-fold stratified cross-validation; primary performance metric: area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC); additional metrics: precision, recall, sensitivity, specificity, balanced accuracy, area under precision-recall curve; permutation testing (1000 permutations) to assess statistical significance of AUROC values against chance-level performance (p < .05); feature importance analysis based on LR coefficients (standardized magnitude indicates strength, sign indicates direction); comparison between models using permutation-based approach with 1000 permuted datasets
clinical_application_and_analysis_part.caa8_key_findings_brief: Cerebellar normative features moderately predicted ASD and SZ (AUROC 0.56-0.65) but not BD, MCI, or AD, with contributions from both anterior and posterior cerebellar regions across multiple atlases.
clinical_application_and_analysis_part.caa9_key_findings_detailed: The study found that lobular and voxelwise cerebellar deviation features derived from normative models could moderately discriminate ASD and SZ from reference samples (AUROC values ranging from 0.56 to 0.65), with permutation testing confirming statistical significance. For SZ, the most predictive models centered on median and variance measures within ROIs, with feature importance analyses highlighting vermis IX, left IV, regions associated with verbal fluency and autobiographical recall, left S1 (social-linguistic-spatial) and D1 (demand) regions, and limbic A and somatomotor A networks. For ASD, models based on lobular volumes and voxelwise variance within ROIs were most predictive, with key regions including left VIIB, left crus II, and areas functionally linked to narrative, emotion, and language processing. In contrast, prediction performance for MCI, AD, and BD did not exceed chance levels, suggesting the cerebellum may be relatively spared in these conditions or that cerebellar features alone are insufficient for prediction. Both anterior (motor-related) and posterior (cognitive-related) cerebellar regions contributed to predictions. No single atlas consistently outperformed others, but using multiple atlases (anatomical, task-based, hierarchical, resting-state) enhanced interpretability. Results were robust across different machine learning methods (LR, RF, XGBoost).

caa10_key_limitations.answer: Limited predictive power (AUROC 0.56-0.65); challenges in harmonizing behavioral, cognitive, genetic, phenotypic, lifestyle, symptomatology, and medical history data across datasets; clinical heterogeneity complicating classification; interpretation of individual-level deviations (biological significance vs. imaging artifacts); subgroup existence within heterogeneous conditions like ASD; appropriateness of adult template space and atlases for younger children and adolescents; lack of multimodal approach and comparison with whole-brain models; manual inspection limited to ~5% of scans; limitations in depicting different atlases with varying borders; challenges in obtaining precise cerebellar MRI data due to distinct skull position and intricate folding pattern
caa10_key_limitations.supporting_text: The limited predictive power of the trained machine learning models (84) should be taken into consideration when interpreting the current findings... harmonizing behavioral, cognitive, genetic, phenotypic, lifestyle, symptomatology, and medical history data across various datasets poses significant challenges... accurately classifying complex clinical conditions is challenging due to the intrinsic heterogeneity of these conditions... The key challenge in normative modeling lies in interpreting deviations at the individual level. The central question is whether these deviations are biologically significant or merely artifacts resulting from signal dropout during imaging... the existence of subgroups within heterogeneous conditions, such as ASD, complicates the interpretation of performance metrics... Neurodevelopmental changes raise concerns about the appropriateness of applying adult template space and atlases to younger children and adolescents (86). Including other key brain regions and utilizing a multimodal approach that integrates different types of brain imaging data may improve predictions (87,88)... Given the large sample size, we manually inspected about 5% of the scans to maintain quality control. Nevertheless, we acknowledge the limitations in accurately depicting different atlases with varying border including lobular segmentation. The cerebellum's distinct position within the skull and its intricate folding pattern also present challenges in obtaining precise MRI data.

clinical_application_and_analysis_part.caa11_application_notes: The study employed four different cerebellar atlases (28-region anatomical, 10-region task-based, 32-region hierarchical, 17-region resting-state) to enhance interpretability of findings. Matched controls were created using nearest-neighbor matching based on exact matches of sex and scanning site with age. Variance of z-scores was used as a novel feature to examine structural heterogeneity. The percentage of extreme deviation (|z| > 1.96) differs from variance by specifically targeting extreme outliers rather than overall dispersion. Only baseline scans were used when participants had multiple timepoints.

general_note_part.gn1_general_notes: This study represents an application of a previously published cerebellar normative model (Kim et al. 2024, reference 15) to prediction tasks rather than development of a new normative model. The normative model evaluation metrics (explained variance, mean squared log loss, skew, kurtosis) were calculated on the test set that did not include clinical cohorts. Four different cerebellar atlases were compared: anatomical (28 ROIs from cerebellar anatomical atlas), task-based (10 ROIs from multidomain task battery by King et al. 2019), hierarchical (32 ROIs from Nettekoven et al. 2024), and resting-state (17 ROIs from Buckner et al. 2011 and Yeo et al. 2011). The study focused exclusively on cerebellar features and did not include cerebral/cortical features, representing a test of cerebellar-specific contribution to prediction. Intensity normalization was performed to range (0,1). Voxelwise models involved ~143,000 voxels organized into different ROI parcellations depending on the atlas. Quality control threshold was based on empirical testing showing non-significant differences between 1 and 2 lobule thresholds for exclusion.
